summary: Documents a simple experiment of a TCP sender using a four-packet start toward a receiver behind a 9600 bps modem link with only three buffers. The finding was that no significant degradation was seen compared with a smaller start. It is informational.

eli5.summary: What happens if you pour four cups of water into a funnel that holds three? This memo tried it with network packets and found things still worked fine.

questions: what happens when tcp sends four packets into three buffers
does a larger tcp initial window hurt slow links
does a four packet tcp start hurt slow modem links
what is the tcp four packet start
subtitle: A small simulation checks whether a four-packet TCP start hurts when a slow modem link has only three buffers.

tldr.problem: Starting TCP with four packets might fail on a slow modem link whose router holds only three packets, because the fourth packet is sure to be dropped.
tldr.mechanism: The authors simulated a sender behind 100 Mbps, 1.5 Mbps and 9600 bps links, comparing a one-packet start with a four-packet start.
tldr.outcome: The two runs reached nearly the same state, and the four-packet start came out slightly ahead, so in this case it is not harmful. The authors say whether it is safe for the network is still an open question.

today: RFC 2416 is an Informational report and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. The proposal it examines is documented in RFC 2414.

sections.title: The Concern Behind the Experiment
sections.content:
Sally Floyd proposed that TCP begin its initial slow start by sending as many as four packets instead of one, to get up to speed faster. Slow starts caused by timeouts would still begin with one packet. A larger start might cut start-up latency over long-fat pipes by two round-trip times.

On the end2end-interest mailing list, someone raised a worry: a slow modem is often served by a router that allocates only three buffers per modem (one packet being sent, two waiting). A four-packet start would then lose the fourth packet for sure. Vern Paxson replied that this is no worse than normal slow start after two round trips, which also releases four closely spaced packets. The experiment confirmed his reasoning.
sections.eli5: Some people feared that a router with room for only three packets would choke on four at once. Another person said normal TCP ends up doing that anyway a little later.

sections.title: The Simulated Network
sections.content:
The scenario has three links between sender and receiver: a 100 Mbps link with no delay (where the authors log ACKs), a 1.5 Mbps link with 25 ms one-way delay, and a 9600 bps link with 150 ms one-way delay. Queue limits on the 9600 bps link were 3 packets, which hold at most two while one is being sent. Other queue limits were 100.

The runs used version 1.2a2 of the NS simulator, with packets of 1024 bytes. The authors tried the tahoe, reno, sack and fack TCP algorithms and believe the conclusion holds for all, using tahoe to illustrate. In the four-packet runs, the window-init variable was 4, and the TCP code was changed to use it only at connection start and to set cwnd to 1 for later slow starts.
sections.eli5: They pretended there was a fast road, then a medium road, then a very slow narrow lane at the end with room for only three packets waiting.

sections.title: Comparing the Two Starts
sections.content:
With a normal slow start, packet 1 goes out at time 0.0 and the first ACK arrives at 1.222, releasing packets 2 and 3. After a few rounds, duplicate ACKs covering packet 6 arrive, and at time 8.278 the third duplicate triggers retransmission of packet 7.

With a four-packet start, packets 1 to 4 go out at time 0.0. Duplicate ACKs covering packet 3 arrive, and at time 5.389 the third one triggers retransmission of packet 4.

From there the two traces are almost the same, shifted by 2.889 seconds and three packets. Sending three 1024-byte segments through a 9600 bps modem takes 2.66 seconds, so the four-packet start delivers packet N about 0.229 seconds earlier than the one-packet start, roughly one fifth of a packet. The extra time comes from the modem sitting idle while the receiver's dally timer runs in the one-packet case.
sections.eli5: Both ways ended up in nearly the same place after losing a packet. The fast start actually got there a tiny bit sooner.

sections.title: Conclusion and Open Questions
sections.content:
The memo concludes that in this particular case the four-packet start is not harmful. The authors add their opinions: it would help a lot on long-delay links, reducing transfer times for moderately sized transfers by as much as two round-trip times, but whether it is safe for the network is still an open question.

They would like the result duplicated with real TCPs, real modems and real three-buffer limits. The security section says the study has no security considerations of its own.
sections.eli5: Verdict: not harmful in this test. They still want someone to try it with real equipment before being sure.

references.text: Allman, M., Floyd, S., and C. Partridge, "Increasing TCP's Initial Window", RFC 2414, September 1998.
S. Floyd, Increasing TCP's Initial Window (January 29, 1997).
